title: A disabled theatre troupe makes the able-bodied the discriminated minority — and it isn't asking for your sympathy
dek: Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the unaugmented able-bodied minority become the original sinners who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a complaint — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.
why: Mostly oral testimony, with no data or research framework; the value is in the concrete scenes and in how a single play grew. Anyone looking for methodology or industry judgment can skip it.
who: People working in public welfare, theatre and community workshops; content people who want to understand why integration can't rely on goodwill alone; practitioners and volunteers in disability issues.
skip: The rehearsal clip at the start and the submission voice-over at the end can be skipped.

points.h: Disabled women being unable to leave the house is a widespread phenomenon
points.body: Yaoyao's earliest work was the documentary Jackdaw (“寒鸦”), about three disabled women's struggles with family education and employment. One of the sisters had not left her home for 36 years; when her parents took her out to visit relatives during holidays, what she felt was ‘like walking a little dog or cat’. Later she got her first computer, went online, and found a job as a telephone operator — no degree required, only a sweet voice — and after getting the job she bought herself a wheelchair and left the house in it. Another visually impaired mother was allowed to breastfeed her baby for only five minutes before her mother-in-law took the child away, on the grounds that ‘you can't see, you can't raise a child’; for years afterward she fought her husband's family for custody. These oral accounts made Yaoyao realise that being unable to leave the house was not an isolated case.

points.h: Disabled people's friends are all disabled people
points.body: A former colleague of Yaoyao's uses a wheelchair, and when she moved she could only ask friends who also use wheelchairs; the chairs were piled front and back with things, cartload after cartload. Yaoyao instinctively asked why she didn't call able-bodied friends who can walk upright to help — it would be done in half a day. The other woman was stunned for a moment and said, I don't know any able-bodied people — she did not have a single able-bodied friend, and even her friends all used wheelchairs. Yaoyao said she didn't know how to continue the conversation, and only realised one thing: if disabled and able-bodied people don't even have the chance to meet, ‘you have no chance of integration at all’. This was the direct starting point for her later search for a drama teacher and her work in integrated theatre.

points.h: Writing able-bodied people as the discriminated original sinners
points.body: The Leyi troupe's first play, Reverse Future (“逆转未来”), does a direct identity reversal: a nuclear war turns most people disabled, and they become new humans through technological modification such as electronic eyes and cochlear implants; the remaining able-bodied minority, because of ‘the crime of starting the nuclear war’, become original sinners, marginalised by society. Yaoyao's logic was that since she herself is a mirror-image person, she might as well flip the whole society too, turning all the rights disabled people now have to fight for into rights able-bodied people have to fight for — she calls this writing a power fantasy for disabled people. The core of the plot: an original-sinner father, to keep his son from suffering again because of an able-bodied body, gets drunk, picks up a chainsaw and tries to saw off his son's legs, but ends up in a pool of blood himself; the son is charged with patricide, and the courtroom scenes bring out the debate about original sinners and augmented humans.

points.h: How the unseen and the unheard partner up
points.body: Visually impaired actor Wang Xiaomin was pulled in by deaf actor Li Ning during an audition to be his partner; his first reaction was confusion: you can't hear, I can't see, how are we supposed to act. Li Ning's solution was to put his hand on the back of Wang's hand and trace, tapping once when it was Wang's turn to speak. Director Ma Yan said that abroad there is already a form of blind and deaf performers on stage together, with the deaf person's hand on the visually impaired person's hand, so the visually impaired person can feel the movements. Wang Xiaomin said that he had been around deaf people since childhood, but back then he thought these were two kinds of people born with communication barriers, ‘it was absolutely impossible for them to communicate’, and the barrier was almost insurmountable — after this collaboration he and Li Ning became very good friends. The troupe also had to solve sign language interpretation, real-time subtitle screens, and assigning a volunteer to each visually impaired actor for audio description.

points.h: Visually impaired actors wear earphones on stage to cheat
points.body: Only later in rehearsals did the director discover that the visually impaired actors were in fact ‘cheating’: they wore earphones, listened to their lines at several times normal speed, and then delivered them seamlessly on stage, so the director had no way to assess them and only wondered how the visually impaired actors got their lines down so fast. Conversely, the director didn't know sign language and could only watch everyone signing while laughing on the side, when in fact the actors might be complaining about him in sign language. Once they got to know each other, everyone's little tricks became known.

points.h: She received the best production award in the ICU
points.body: In 2024 Reverse Future was selected for the Nanjing New Theatre Festival initiated by Stan Lai. That year Yaoyao had heart problems and was in the ICU; the troupe nearly fell apart, and it was a friend who stepped in to gather everyone for rehearsals and take them to Nanjing. At the closing buffet, while the other groups' tables were empty and everyone was dressed up waiting for the awards, only their table kept going back for more after finishing, thinking ‘how could it possibly be us’. In the end they won the Best Production award, the highest prize at the Nanjing New Theatre Festival, and jury chairman Stan Lai stood up and led the applause. At the same moment the news reached the ICU, and Yaoyao lay in her hospital bed in tears. In October of the same year the play was specially invited to the Wuzhen Theatre Festival, as the first integrated disability production, and became the only production in the ‘Nothing Is Impossible’ section.

points.h: After writing this play, she changed her answer and chose not to be born
points.body: The second play, I Choose to Be Born (“我选择出生”), is set in a world where every country legislates that when a fetus reaches eight months, parents must use brainwaves to inform it of its health condition and family environment, and the fetus decides whether to be born. Among five families, there are deaf parents who must truthfully tell their child that you will be deaf too, a husband who deceives his wife into having a child, a family that favours boys over girls, and the last story is adapted from Yaoyao's own experience. The troupe's actors couldn't get through the script because their life experiences were so eerily similar, only the illnesses differed. Asked whether they would still choose to be born if they had the chance to do it over, most of the troupe still said they would choose birth, because they still love this world; but Yaoyao changed her answer: she used to say she would choose birth too, but now she might choose not to be born, because disabled people are forced to be born into this society, with no choice.

points.h: The same question, Cai Cong and she give opposite answers
points.body: The programme sets the deaf couple in I Choose to Be Born against the real-life Cai Cong: Cai Cong and his wife are both visually impaired, and when his wife was pregnant many people urged them to get tests to see whether the child would inherit the visual impairment, but Cai Cong did not want to presume that such a life was not worth starting merely because the child might also be visually impaired; they believe they can give a child a loving family. The deaf couple in the play decide to let the child be born. Yaoyao and Cai Cong give very different answers, and the debate around this choice has always existed. The question the programme poses is: when a family makes a choice, how much choice do they actually have?
